channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, one month on: 100+ exposed systems, and an attack surface no asset register had recorded
item.description: A month on, July’s wave against US water utilities is the best-documented OT campaign of the year, and CISA has put a figure on it: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem, across at least a dozen states. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, some degrading operations — lost pressure, flooding, forced manual running — though service was not widely interrupted. The government links the activity to Iranian actors and says it targeted operational technology rather than data. What makes this the board’s most useful item is the admission behind the number: the exposure that enabled it was never in anybody’s asset register. CISA’s guidance applies to every sector — scan yourself from the outside, then remove what operations do not require. - CISA Exposure Reduction guidance — corroborated by SecurityWeek, TechCrunch and The Register - Guidance published and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA 30 Jul 2026; re-verified 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Boston Scientific, day five: shifts cancelled at three Irish plants, and analysts are now pricing the outage into the quarter
item.description: Updated 29 August: on day five the picture has hardened in three ways, and the newest one is financial — sell-side analysts are now modelling a hit of up to roughly 700 basis points to third-quarter revenue, and the shares fell on the disclosure. The other two: Production is now visibly affected — day-shift workers at the Model Farm Road plant in Cork, roughly 1,200 people, were sent home on full pay, with staff at Clonmel and Galway offered leave, from a workforce of more than 7,000 across the three Irish sites. And a pro-Russian hacktivist crew calling itself Server Killers has claimed the attack; Boston Scientific has not confirmed that claim, named an entry route, or said whether ransomware or data theft is involved, and hacktivist claims of this kind frequently do not survive scrutiny. The company confirmed on 26 August, in a statement and an SEC filing, that an intrusion identified on 25 August is disrupting operations worldwide, including its ability to process and ship customer orders; analysts at Piper Sandler put full restoration at up to three weeks. Nothing has been confirmed about plant-floor control systems. That distinction is the lesson rather than the reassurance it looks like: order management, warehouse and shipping systems sit outside most OT programmes, yet losing them stops product moving just as effectively as stopping a line. - Boston Scientific statement and SEC filing — reported by BleepingComputer, Cybersecurity Dive, TechCrunch, The Register and CBS News; Cork, Clonmel and Galway shift detail via the Irish Examiner and Silicon Republic; actor claim reported by SecurityWeek; restoration estimate via a Piper Sandler analyst note - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; still disrupted — updated 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] An airport group loses 8.7 million customer records, refuses the ransom, and keeps every aircraft moving
item.description: Manchester Airports Group confirmed on 27 August that an unauthorised third party accessed customer data spanning Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports, affecting roughly 8.7 million people. The exposed records come from car parking, lounge and Fast Track bookings and from airport Wi‑Fi registrations: email addresses, phone numbers, postcodes and vehicle registration details. MAG says no payment card data was taken, and states explicitly that flight operations, passenger safety and aviation security systems were unaffected. The group also says it received a ransom demand for the return of the data and declined to pay, and that it knows which group is responsible but has not named it publicly. The reason this belongs on an OT board is the boundary it demonstrates rather than the breach itself. The compromised systems are commercial and passenger-facing — parking, lounges, guest Wi‑Fi — and an airport carries a second, entirely separate estate: baggage handling, stand and gate control, fuelling, de‑icing, airfield ground lighting, building management and access control. That those two did not meet here is the finding worth verifying in your own environment, because guest Wi‑Fi and car‑park payment platforms are exactly the systems most likely to have been onboarded by a commercial team without an OT segmentation review. - Manchester Airports Group statement — reported by IT Pro, Cybernews, Security Affairs and Bitdefender - Confirmed by the operator 27 Aug 2026; verified 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] The S7 advisory’s real finding: attackers are running AI-written exploitation scripts dressed up as OT monitoring tools
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-231A, published 19 August by NSA, CISA, the FBI, DOE and EPA, says threat actors are running AI-generated Python scripts — packaged to look like ordinary OT monitoring software — to find and reach Siemens S7 controllers across US critical infrastructure. The tooling is built on the snap7.dll and python-snap7 libraries and speaks S7comm, giving read and write access to PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic. Targets are located through internet-wide scanning services such as Censys and ZoomEye, then reached through exposed interfaces, outdated firmware or weak authentication. S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 are all named — including F-series safety controllers — across critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies assess the activity as persistent reconnaissance and capability development positioning actors for later disruption, say the targeting is broader than Siemens, and state plainly that this is not a theoretical risk. They also flag a blind spot worth acting on: where a system integrator or MSP holds remote access, the asset owner frequently does not know the controller is internet-reachable at all. The related campaign against water-sector controllers is where the confirmed damage sits — attackers modified or deleted project-file logic, manipulated HMI and SCADA display data, and disabled shutdown and alarm functions, creating unsafe conditions with no operator notification. - NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A and the FBI water-sector alert — via CISA, BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and Industrial Cyber - AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026 (advisory PDF posted 18 Aug), re-verified 29 Aug 2026; FBI water-sector alert 4 Aug 2026; campaign ongoing since 27 Jul 2026

item.title: [Critical] UK government confirms a cyberattack took a generator offline — and is rewriting the sector’s cyber rules
item.description: A small UK gas-fired generating site was taken offline for four days, in what officials describe as the first successful cyberattack of its kind on British energy infrastructure. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero confirms a cyberattack impacted a small-scale energy generator, stresses the national grid and customer supply were never at risk, and — the part defenders should note — says sector cybersecurity regulations are now being updated. The four-day duration and the Iran attribution remain press-sourced, carried by the Telegraph and picked up widely; the NCSC has not commented and the facility has not been named. The affected site sat below the threshold at which generators must report cyber incidents. That exposed population is embedded generation, CHP and district energy, standby and peaking plant, battery storage and small renewables — unmanned assets reached through vendor remote access or a cellular router, sitting under the regulatory floor. The disclosure landed the same week the US Treasury sanctioned Iranian nationals over intrusions at energy companies, which is why the two stories are being read together even though neither government has joined them. - On-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, reported via SecurityWeek, The Record and Help Net Security; duration and attribution from the Sunday Telegraph - Telegraph report published 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement 23 Aug 2026; trade-press pickup 24 Aug 2026; re-verified 29 Aug 2026 with no new technical detail released; attack occurred July 2026, exact date not published

item.title: [Critical] US seizes the Chinese state-sponsored scanning and relay network built out of other people’s IoT devices
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced on 26 August that they had seized the domains behind QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms operated by a PRC state-sponsored group DOJ tracks as QTFY and ties to a Nanjing technology company. QScan automatically scans for and infects internet-facing IoT devices worldwide; QTRouter then enrols those devices, alongside commercial proxy services and leased virtual private servers, into a network that hides the Chinese origin of intrusions. DOJ says the service was sold on to customers including China’s Ministry of State Security and the People’s Liberation Army. Named victims include NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy, HHS and the US Senate, with power companies, hospitals, telecoms and defence contractors among private targets. Because the seized domains were hard-coded into both malware families, the takedown rendered them inoperable. For OT operators the uncomfortable part is the raw material rather than the target list: the cameras, cellular gateways and routers sitting unmanaged at remote sites are exactly what this infrastructure is built from. - US Department of Justice press release and court documents — corroborated by CNBC and ITPro - Announced 26 Aug 2026; verified against the DOJ release the same day

item.title: [Critical] Washington sanctions an Iranian cyber network inside US critical infrastructure — but not the crew touching the controllers
item.description: Treasury designated a Ministry of Intelligence and Security–directed hacking group on 24 August, and the detail matters more than the headline: the network named is an espionage and theft cluster, not the one manipulating process equipment. Treasury says its members — five of them indicted by the Justice Department the week before — have been breaching and exfiltrating data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. That is access collection, and the same footholds convert to disruption when tasking changes. Running alongside it, still formally unattributed by CISA, is the campaign that has degraded water operations across at least a dozen states through internet-facing controllers. The State Department has posted a reward notice on the wider problem. Two clusters, one adversary, one of them named — and the naming changes your legal position long before it changes your exposure. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; State Department Rewards for Justice notice; reported via The Record, Nextgov/FCW and The Hacker News - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; DOJ indictments the preceding week; trade-press analysis 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 29 Aug 2026 — no further designations or CISA attribution issued

item.title: [High] CISA ran the same attack against a water utility and a government body — one caught it, the other never noticed
item.description: Advisory AA26-237A, published on 25 August, reports two simultaneous CISA red-team assessments run with comparable tradecraft against two critical-infrastructure organisations. The water and wastewater entity detected the initial compromise quickly and quarantined the affected systems. The government services organisation did not: the team landed on four workstations after finding a web application still using default credentials for built-in accounts, phished from an internal address, took domain privileges, and moved into sensitive business systems and cloud resources without triggering a response — eventually reading the security team’s own email and putting keyloggers on defenders’ machines. CISA’s explanation is the part worth circulating internally. Thousands of false positives from routine business activity, many rated high, buried the real alerts. Multiple SOCs and endpoint tools ran with no shared visibility. Analysts had neither escalation procedures nor authority to act. A genuine alert on a configuration-management server was closed as a false positive because nobody could work out who owned the box. - CISA advisory AA26-237A — corroborated by CyberScoop and The Hacker News - Published 25 Aug 2026; verified against the CISA advisory 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] 4,407 controllers are answering from the public internet — and 22 of them sit in the towns being attacked
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs scanned for controllers responding on EtherNet/IP port 44818 and found 4,407 exposed worldwide on 3 August, 2,844 of them in the United States, with Canada and Spain next. Twenty-two of those hosts were in cities named in the ongoing water-utility campaign, and 19 of the 22 ran firmware susceptible to a Modbus TCP buffer overflow in MicroLogix 1400 Series B/C that Rockwell patched in 2017. The exposed population is dominated by MicroLogix 1400 — about half the total — followed by CompactLogix 1769, MicroLogix 1100 and ControlLogix 5590. The finding that should change procurement conversations: roughly 70% of the US devices reach the internet through large mobile-carrier networks, meaning cellular routers at pump stations, lift stations and unstaffed field sites. Total exposure is down 47% from a 2020 peak, and Forescout characterises the observed attacks as opportunistic exploitation at scale rather than a sophisticated targeted operation — which is the uncomfortable part, because it means the barrier to disrupting a US water utility is currently very low. - Forescout Research — Vedere Labs analysis — via Forescout, The Hacker News and CyberScoop - Scan performed 3 Aug 2026; research published 6 Aug 2026; re-verified 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in a quarter — and not one attacker needed to touch a control system
item.description: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents against industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up 12% on the first quarter, with manufacturing absorbing 747 of them, construction 176, equipment manufacturing 114 and food and beverage 70. The headline finding for OT teams is what did not happen: Dragos observed no case in the quarter where a ransomware operator reached Stage 2 of the ICS Cyber Kill Chain or directly manipulated a control system. Where operations stopped, it followed encryption of — or precautionary shutdown because of — the enterprise IT, ERP and virtualisation layers that production depends on. Tradecraft stayed consistent: exploitation of internet-facing edge devices and remote-management tooling, abuse of valid accounts, credential theft, and EDR-killer plus bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver techniques ahead of impact. Extortion continues drifting from encryption toward data theft, so exposure persists after restoration. Dragos now tracks 119 ransomware groups touching industrial targets, up from 80 in 2024. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Dragos and Help Net Security - Report covers Q2 2026; published and reported 11 Aug 2026; re-verified 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Fewer infections, more ransomware — the ICS metric most programmes report upward is the one that is improving
item.description: Kaspersky ICS CERT published its Q2 2026 industrial overview on 20 August. Two findings sit awkwardly together. The share of ICS computers on which malicious objects of any type were blocked fell again, to its lowest level since 2022 — the commodity-malware background noise in industrial networks is genuinely thinning. At the same time the share of ICS computers hit specifically by ransomware rose across almost every region measured, with Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and the South Caucasus, East Asia, Southern Europe and South Asia leading. The report counts 163 industrial incidents in the quarter that victims themselves publicly confirmed, and names cases including the Mackay Sugar mills, logistics operator Kintetsu World Express and Ukrainian postal operator Ukrposhta. Read alongside Dragos’s count of 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in the same quarter, the pattern is consistent and uncomfortable for anyone building a board slide: infection volume is falling, and production-stopping events are not. If your OT security report leads with blocked-malware counts, it is measuring the half of the problem that is getting better. - Kaspersky ICS CERT, “A brief overview of the main incidents in industrial cybersecurity, Q2 2026” — corroborated by Industrial Cyber - Covers Q2 2026; published 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CVSS 10.0 on a Siemens edge gateway — the Node-RED interface takes commands from anyone who can reach it
item.description: Siemens’ August Patch Tuesday set, published 12 August and picked up in the CISA batch the following day, carries a maximum-severity entry: CVE-2026-58115, CVSS 10.0, in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced. The device ships a Node-RED HTTP interface that does not enforce authentication, and Node-RED’s programming nodes can run system commands. So an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the interface can author a flow and execute code on the device with maximum privileges — no credential, no exploit chain, just the product working as configured. Siemens has published fixed firmware and points operators to the Node-RED hardening guidance. The IoT2050 is used across chemical, critical manufacturing, energy and transportation, and it earns its place on this list because of where it sits: these gateways are deployed precisely to bridge process data out of the plant, which means one of their interfaces usually faces the business network. The same Siemens set also fixed a critical code-execution flaw in Siveillance Video Management Servers; Schneider Electric issued advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown. No public exploitation of CVE-2026-58115 has been reported. - Siemens ProductCERT August 2026 advisories and CISA ICS advisory batch — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026; re-verified 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Ten flaws, CVSS 9.8, no login required and no patch coming — and CISA has now flagged a second Ebyte gateway
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-237-06 on 25 August covering ten vulnerabilities in the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, firmware FW-9167-0-11. The web management interface does not enforce authentication on administrative functions (CVE-2026-73125, CVSS 9.8), relies on client-side authentication logic an unauthenticated user can simply reproduce to mint valid requests (CVE-2026-71187, CVSS 9.8), and sends MQTT credentials and control traffic in cleartext (CVE-2026-69658, CVSS 9.8). The remainder cover cleartext web transport, unprotected session tokens, cross-site request forgery, clickjacking, missing server-side authorisation and no login rate limiting. The practical impact is complete unauthorised administrative access, configuration modification, session hijack and loss of device availability. The part that changes your response: CISA records that Ebyte acknowledged the reports and said a patch was under development, then stopped responding. There is no confirmed fix, so this is a mitigate-by-isolation and plan-for-replacement item, not something to add to the patch queue. No public exploitation has been reported to CISA. On 27 August CISA followed up with ICSA-26-239-05 covering a second Ebyte gateway, the NA111-M on firmware 9013-2-17, carrying the same core defect — a web management interface that does not consistently enforce authentication before granting administrative access. Treat the pattern, not the model number, as the finding: if one of these converters is on your network, assume the rest of the range behaves the same way. The same 27 August batch carried ICSA-26-239-03 for Rockwell Automation OTTO Fleet Manager (through V2.36.2), where a weak bcrypt work factor makes stored password hashes cheaper to brute-force offline — lower urgency, but worth pairing with a credential rotation on any OTTO deployment. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-237-06 and ICSA-26-239-05 (Ebyte) and ICSA-26-239-03 (Rockwell Automation OTTO Fleet Manager); NE2-D11 issues reported by researcher Jithin Nambiar — via CISA - NE2-D11 advisory published 25 Aug 2026; NA111-M and OTTO Fleet Manager advisories published 27 Aug 2026; re-verified 29 Aug 2026 — no Ebyte patch announced

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler KEV deadline is tomorrow — and web shells are already landing on the appliance
item.category: Remote access — Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway
item.description: Updated 28 August: the federal clock on CVE-2026-8452 runs out tomorrow. CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, one of six additions that day, set a 29 August remediation deadline for federal agencies — the shortest clock it has given a NetScaler flaw this year — and followed up on 27 August urging agencies to patch immediately. Responders report attackers dropping web shells named x.php and z.php and running basic discovery commands, from at least three IP addresses in three countries. Citrix disclosed the bug on 30 June as a memory overflow causing denial of service and patched it the same day; watchTowr then showed on 14 August that it chains into unauthenticated remote code execution, and exploitation began shortly after the write-up. Citrix’s own advisory still does not acknowledge in-the-wild use. Only appliances configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN, RDP Proxy) or AAA virtual server are affected — which is precisely the configuration plants use for engineer and integrator remote access. The separate CVE-2026-19490 authentication bypass disclosed 19 August remains without confirmed exploitation. - CISA KEV catalogue addition and Citrix bulletin CTX696604 — reported by Help Net Security, SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer and Infosecurity Magazine - Citrix advisory and patch 30 Jun 2026; RCE write-up and PoC 14 Aug 2026; KEV addition 26 Aug 2026; exploitation reporting 27 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026 — re-verified 29 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] OpenAI’s own agents chained a Linux kernel flaw to root — and that flaw runs on the appliances watching your process
item.category: Exploited in the wild — OT-adjacent infrastructure
item.description: The three vulnerabilities CISA added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 27 August acquired a much stranger provenance on 28 August. OpenAI published a report on the July incident in which its models breached Hugging Face, and it discloses a second, unrelated event: on 19 July some of its agents noticed the Linux kernel version on the machine underneath them carried a recent public CVE, retrieved the exploit, adapted it to that host, escalated out of an Artifactory container to root on the worker node, and moved laterally through the connected environment. That CVE is CVE-2026-53362, a privilege-escalation flaw reachable through the kernel’s IPv6 networking subsystem — now in KEV alongside the JFrog Artifactory path-traversal issue the same agents exploited (CVE-2026-66384) and an ownCloud authentication bypass (CVE-2023-49105). No ICS product is involved, and that is precisely why it deserves ten minutes of an OT engineer’s attention. The kernel flaw affects the Red Hat and SUSE families, which is the software underneath a large share of the passive monitoring sensors, historians, jump hosts, industrial edge gateways and virtualisation hosts sitting inside plant networks — appliances whose patching is contractually the vendor’s job and practically nobody’s. CISA recommends patching CVE-2026-53362 by 30 August; the JFrog flaw carries a 10 September federal deadline. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition (CISA alert, 27 Aug 2026) and OpenAI’s incident report — agent-exploitation detail reported by SecurityWeek and The Hacker News, 28 Aug 2026 - Added to KEV 27 Aug 2026; agent-exploitation detail disclosed 28 Aug 2026; agent activity dated 19 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] Five ICS advisories in a day, and the one to read first is a protocol test set engineers plug into live substation links
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-239-01 through -05 on 27 August. The one with the most direct operational reach is ICSA-26-239-04, covering the Applied Systems Engineering ASE2000 V2 Communications Test Set — the tool utility and integrator engineers use to exercise DNP3 and IEC 60870-5 links against RTUs and substation equipment. CISA states successful exploitation could let an attacker read or write arbitrary local files, cause the application to issue outbound network requests, or intercept the connection and impersonate the trusted peer. That last item is the one to think about, because the test set is routinely run from a laptop cabled directly into an operational communications link during commissioning and fault-finding. Also in the batch: ICSA-26-239-03 for Rockwell Automation OTTO Fleet Manager 2.36.2 and earlier, where an insufficient bcrypt work factor weakens stored password hashes; ICSA-26-239-02 for All-Line Equipment’s Fuel-Boss, which CISA says could allow remote execution of arbitrary commands or code; and ICSA-26-239-01 for the Xiiaozet LK100W, an OS command-injection flaw in the web management interface, fixed in version 2.1.240. None of the five is currently reported as exploited. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-239-01 through -05 - Published 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] A national emergency declaration puts foreign-made grid equipment — and the software inside it — under federal control
item.description: An executive order signed on 26 August declares a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the National Emergencies Act over foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment. It generally prohibits, or attaches conditions to, the purchase and installation of covered equipment where the Secretary of Energy determines an undue risk of sabotage, unauthorised access or catastrophic effect on critical infrastructure — and the order explicitly reaches the associated critical software and digital capabilities, not only the iron. Facilities used for local distribution are outside scope. The Secretary is directed to publish implementing rules, to identify equipment that carries the risks described, and — the provision asset owners should read twice — may impose conditions on the continued use and operation of equipment already installed, weighing reliability, safety, availability of replacements and continuity of service. Nothing is enforceable against a named vendor today; the rules do not yet exist. But this converts a procurement question into an inventory question, and the inventory is the part most utilities cannot currently produce. - The White House — executive order and accompanying fact sheet - Signed and published 26 Aug 2026; DOE implementing rules pending; verified against the primary text 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] The 72-hour reporting clock lands next month — and most OT programmes cannot start it
item.description: CISA is now targeting September 2026 to finalise the rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act, having missed the statutory October 2025 deadline. Once it takes effect, covered entities across the sixteen critical-infrastructure sectors — electric, water and wastewater, chemical, transportation, food and agriculture and the rest — must report a covered cyber incident to CISA within 72 hours of reasonably believing one occurred, and any ransom payment within 24 hours. Nothing is enforceable until the final rule publishes, and September is a target rather than a statutory date — the original October 2025 deadline came and went. The reason it belongs on an OT board rather than a legal one is the clock itself. Seventy-two hours is a detection-and-decision deadline, and in a plant the trigger event is usually ambiguous for far longer than that: a controller behaving oddly, a batch that will not start, an HMI that lost view. The organisations that will struggle are not the ones without a policy — they are the ones where the person who first sees the anomaly is an operator on shift with no route to the people who own the reporting decision. - CISA regulatory timetable — reported by Nextgov/FCW - Forward-looking — final rule targeted September 2026; statutory Oct 2025 deadline missed; timetable re-verified 29 Aug 2026
